title: Faster Isn’t Free: The Real Trade-offs of Quantizing a Model from FP32 to INT8
summary: How to evaluate INT8 quantization honestly by measuring latency, output fidelity, calibration coverage, and production risk.
author: Shubham Anandani
body:
I’ve shipped CPU-only inference, and I’ve also declined to ship a “faster” model when the trade-off did not hold up. Quantizing a model from FP32 to INT8 can help meet latency or memory goals. It can also change outputs in ways that matter to the people relying on them.

In my public demo, aceu-edge-infer, I use a small ONNX classifier converted to OpenVINO IR and maintain FP32 and INT8 variants. The service reports which precision it used. It returns four ACE-U dimensions—Authenticity, Credibility, Empathy, and Uniqueness—but these are illustrative outputs from a demo, not validated judgments of real people. The engineering questions are the useful part.

Why quantization can help—and why it changes behavior

Quantization represents selected model weights and activations using lower-precision values. With fewer bits to move and process, an inference path may use less memory and run faster on compatible hardware. The actual speedup depends on the model, operators, runtime, and target device; INT8 is not a universal fast switch.

Lower precision also introduces rounding. Small changes in early layers can flow through later layers, and a score close to a decision threshold may move across it. Some operators quantize cleanly; others may need different quantization settings, to remain in higher precision, or to run through a fallback path.

Look for where the errors gather

Aggregate accuracy can hide concentrated regressions. Compare FP32 and INT8 outputs by class and by meaningful input slice. Inspect examples near decision boundaries, rare patterns, and values near the extremes of the calibration distribution. A useful audit asks not only “How much did the average score move?” but also “Where did the model change its decision?”

Calibrate on data that resembles use

Post-training quantization uses calibration samples to estimate ranges for activations. If the samples do not resemble the inputs the service will see, those ranges can be a poor fit. Include representative cases and the edge cases you care about. When real data cannot be used, diverse synthetic examples can help exercise the pipeline, but they do not replace evaluation on an appropriate held-out set.

A minimal OpenVINO/NNCF sketch looks like this. calibration_samples must yield preprocessed examples in the model’s expected input format:

import nncf
import openvino as ov

core = ov.Core()
model = core.read_model("model_fp32.xml")
calibration_dataset = nncf.Dataset(calibration_samples)

model_int8 = nncf.quantize(model, calibration_dataset)
ov.save_model(model_int8, "model_int8.xml")

This produces a quantized model; it does not establish that the model is accurate enough for a particular use. Keep calibration data and evaluation data separate, and record the evaluation results alongside the model artifact.

Measure more than a mean

  • Latency distribution: report p50, p95, and p99 for both precisions. A mean alone can hide a worse tail.
  • Output deltas: compare score changes and decision changes across the evaluation set.
  • Warm-up: exclude initialization and compilation work from steady-state measurements, but report cold-start behavior separately if it matters in production.
  • Representative conditions: use the same device, request shape, batch size, concurrency, and preprocessing path.

The demo contains a small harness that runs synthetic requests against both variants. Its results are scaffolding until measured on an appropriate workload; synthetic measurements should never be presented as production performance.

Know when not to ship INT8

If the latency improvement is marginal while the output changes affect a high-importance class, the trade-off may be negative. For sensitive applications, stability can matter more than a modest speed gain. Compare other options too: batching, request scheduling, a different CPU pool, or optimizing a costly preprocessing step may achieve the goal with less model-level change.

Make precision visible and roll out in steps

Record the precision and execution device in service logs or response metadata so a change is diagnosable. Keep the public response contract minimal and avoid exposing sensitive implementation details.

Before a full rollout, run FP32 and INT8 in shadow for a representative sample and alert on meaningful divergence. If one slice regresses, route it back to FP32 or disable the INT8 path while you investigate. Maintaining both variants adds operational work, but gives the team a controlled recovery option.

Try it yourself

  1. Build FP32 and INT8 variants and disclose the precision used for each request.
  2. Measure warm and cold paths separately, then report latency percentiles and output-delta distributions.
  3. Evaluate by class and edge-case slice, not only by aggregate accuracy.
  4. Run a shadow comparison and define in advance what divergence will trigger a rollback.

Closing thought

Quantization is powerful, but faster is not free. Percentiles, output deltas, and slice-level evaluation tell you whether INT8 belongs in the production path—or whether FP32 is the more responsible choice.

Further reading

  • OpenVINO post-training quantization overview
  • NNCF basic quantization flow and calibration datasets
  • OpenVINO CPU device and supported inference precisions

title: Designing for Partial Data: Distinguishing “We Don’t Know” From “False”
summary: Model “unknown” separately from “false.” Learn sealed types, exhaustive pattern matching, and propagation rules that preserve meaning end to end.
author: Shubham Anandani
body:
Partial data is normal. Missing signals and unverifiable sources happen. If you collapse “unknown” into “false” or “zero,” you erode trust. As an engineering manager, I’ve learned to design services that treat “we don’t know” as a first-class outcome. In Java, sealed types and exhaustive pattern matching make this straightforward and enforceable.

The failure mode

Your aggregator treats null as “0.0,” sums four dimensions, and displays a neat number. A caller misreads that as “complete and low.” In reality, two dimensions were missing, and one was unverifiable. The number masked uncertainty.

What I learned

Keep partial states in the domain layer, not just at the edges

Don’t convert unknowns to defaults at the boundary. Let domain logic operate on sealed types. If you must produce a single number, force policy conversion in a dedicated function so that the decision is auditable.

Policy example

public final class AggregationPolicy {
public static double conservativeAverage(List<ScoreOrUnknown> dims) {
int count = 0;
double sum = 0.0;
for (ScoreOrUnknown d : dims) {
switch (d) {
case Score sc         -> { sum += sc.value(); count++; }
case Missing miss     -> { /* exclude; track missing elsewhere */ }
case Unverifiable unv -> { /* exclude; track unverifiable */ }
}
}
if (count == 0) return Double.NaN; // no numeric evidence
return sum / count;
}
public static boolean okToDisplay(List<ScoreOrUnknown> dims) {
long unknowns = dims.stream().filter(x -> !(x instanceof Score)).count();
return unknowns == 0; // or choose a threshold
}
}

Propagate uncertainty deliberately

Unknowns should travel with the data: into logs, decisions, and UI. For example, if two dimensions are unknown, surface that count alongside any numeric aggregation. The goal is to prevent silent conversions that distort confidence.

Make unknown-handling policies explicit and testable

Write tests that assert what happens when all dimensions are unknown, when some are missing, and when a single unverifiable dimension appears. Pattern matching keeps these tests aligned with the domain states. Don’t assume a “best effort” numeric default; decide and encode.

Resist “default values” in DTOs

If you serialize to JSON, include a type field in each dimension and omit value when the state isn’t Score. A consumer reading {"type":"Missing","reason":"timeout"} can act accordingly. Defaulting to 0.0 or “unknown=false” invites misuse.

Teach callers to branch by type, not numeric checks Documentation should show switch examples, not “if value is 0 then unknown.” This reduces coupling and preserves room for future states (e.g., “Contested,” “Deprecated”).

Audit conversion points with a linelist List every place where ScoreOrUnknown becomes a single number or a boolean. Audit these conversions periodically. If you discover accidental flattening, refactor to preserve states or add proper policy functions.

Accept that aggregation may return “no number” Returning NaN or omitting a field is reasonable when inputs are fully unknown. Treat this as normal, not exceptional. UI can show “insufficient evidence” with counts; APIs can document this outcome clearly.

JSON serialization with a type field

// Using a simple custom serializer sketch

public record Score(double value) implements ScoreOrUnknown {}
public record Missing(String reason) implements ScoreOrUnknown {}
public record Unverifiable(String note) implements ScoreOrUnknown {}
public Map<String, Object> toJson(ScoreOrUnknown s) {
return switch (s) {
case Score sc         -> Map.of("type", "Score", "value", sc.value());
case Missing miss     -> Map.of("type", "Missing", "reason", miss.reason());
case Unverifiable unv -> Map.of("type", "Unverifiable", "note", unv.note());

};

}

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

Transparency vs brevity: Returning types and reasons increases payload size but improves clarity. Favor clarity when ambiguity matters.

Strictness vs convenience: Throwing on invalid scores and disallowing defaults catches bugs early but may frustrate callers used to flexible shapes.

NaN vs explicit omission: NaN signals “no numeric value” but can be mishandled by consumers. Omitting a field or providing a separate state field avoids confusion.

Failure modes

“Silent flattening”

A downstream transforms unknowns to zero—likely out of habit. Catch this in contract tests.

“Enum drift”

If reason codes evolve, consumers break. Document codes and provide a safe default handling path.

“Partial measures hiding in averages”: An average of one numeric with three unknowns looks “complete” unless you also surface unknown counts.

Try it yourself

Refactor one DTO to embed a sealed state rather than a nullable numeric field. Add a type field in JSON. Update consumers to switch on type.

Write aggregation policies that return NaN or omit fields when inputs are fully unknown. Test behavior explicitly.

Add metrics that count unknowns and unverifiable states separately from numeric distributions.

  • Records (JEP 395)
  • Sealed Classes (JEP 409)
  • Pattern Matching for switch (JEP 441)

title: Flaky Tests Are a Concurrency Bug: Fixing Shared State Under Parallel Execution
summary: Flaky tests often signal shared state bugs. Learn to diagnose parallel execution issues, isolate fixtures, and design for deterministic test behavior.
author: Shubham Anandani
body:
I’ve watched teams chase “test runner bugs” while the real culprit was design. Flakiness is often a concurrency issue—shared mutable state under parallel execution. JUnit 5 can run tests concurrently, so fixtures that share mutable state can make failures appear intermittent. Creating isolated data per test makes the behavior easier to reproduce and diagnose.

The failure mode

You enable parallel test execution and see intermittent failures: “record not found” or “unexpected duplicate.” You re-run and it passes. Blaming the test runner is easy. The problem is shared state: two tests reading/writing the same fixture or relying on an implicit order.

What I learned

Default to per-test fixtures

Use per-test initialization to avoid shared mutable state. In JUnit 5, keep your test instance lifecycle at PER_METHOD and recreate fixtures for each test. If the fixture is expensive, consider a template with parameterization that still isolates state.

Example setup

import org.junit.jupiter.api.*;
@TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_METHOD)
class EvidenceServiceTest {
private InMemoryStore store;
private EvidenceService service;
@BeforeEach
void init() {
store = new InMemoryStore(); // new store per test
service = new EvidenceService(store);
store.seedProfile("alice", syntheticProfileAlice());
}
@Test
void returnsMissingWhenTimeout() {
// ...
}
@Test
void returnsUnverifiableOnExceptions() {
// ...
}
}

Avoid static mutable fields—especially in helpers

Static caches and helpers make tests faster locally but brittle in parallel. If you truly need a cache, scope it per test, or guard it with thread-safe constructs and clear it explicitly. Better: don’t cache at all in tests unless you benchmarked the need.

Make isolation visible—name-bound fixtures

If a test seeds data, bind it to a unique key per test. Use random UUIDs or test names in keys to prevent accidental cross-test reuse. With Testcontainers, create per-test containers when state isolation is critical; share containers only for read-only tests.

Parallel execution deserves explicit design

JUnit 5 lets you run tests in parallel. That doesn’t mean every test should be parallel. Annotate classes that require single-thread execution, but treat that as a last resort. Prefer making tests parallel-safe by design.

JUnit configuration (illustrative):

junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.enabled = true
junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.mode.default = concurrent
junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.mode.classes.default = concurrent

Deterministic time and waiting

Tests that sleep and “hope the system is ready” fail under parallel runs. Replace sleeps with explicit synchronization: await a condition, poll with a small backoff, or use latches. Keep timeouts small and deterministic.

Embrace “given-when-then” with isolated builders

Build input data per test with dedicated builders. Don’t reuse a mutable “default profile” object across tests; copy or reconstruct it. Records help: immutable inputs prevent accidental mutation.

Diagnose with logging and seeds

When a test fails intermittently, print seeds and keys that identify data. If you see the same key in two tests, you found shared state. If you see non-deterministic ordering in a collection, sort inputs or assert set equivalence rather than list order.

Per-test container with unique data

class StoreTests {
    private PostgreSQLContainer<?> database;

    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() {
        database = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:alpine")
            .withDatabaseName("test_" + UUID.randomUUID())
            .withUsername("user")
            .withPassword("test-only");
        database.start();
    }

    @AfterEach
    void tearDown() {
        database.stop();
    }
}

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

Isolation vs speed: Per-test fixtures are slower than shared ones. Optimize later—start with correct behavior and only share read-only fixtures.

Parallelism vs determinism: Parallel runs surface concurrency bugs but may require more careful test design. The benefits outweigh the cost.

Container lifecycle vs developer ergonomics: Per-test containers are robust but slower. Consider class-level containers for read-only tests with clear resets.

Failure modes

“Hidden globals”

A helper modifies a static map. Under parallel, tests interleave and fail intermittently.

“Order assumptions”: Tests rely on iteration order of sets or maps; parallel runs expose different orders.

“Implicit sleeps”: Tests use fixed sleeps; faster/slower environments cause out-of-order expectations.

Try it yourself

Switch to PER_METHOD lifecycle and remove static mutable fields in tests. Add unique keys per test to seed data. Enable parallel execution and watch for failures that indicate hidden shared state.

Replace sleep-based readiness with explicit condition checks. Add timeouts and backoff policies.

Document which tests are parallel-safe and why; make non-parallel tests the exception and note the reason.

Further reading

  • JUnit 5 parallel execution
  • Testcontainers for Java
subtitle: When tests fail intermittently, look for shared mutable fixtures—then fix the design, not just the test runner.

title: Records Aren’t Just Less Typing: Modeling Ambiguity Without Nulls
summary: Modern Java lets you model ambiguity without nulls. Learn records, sealed interfaces, and pattern matching to represent missing and unverifiable states clearly.
author: Shubham Anandani
body:
I’m an engineering manager with a background in Java backend systems. One lesson that keeps paying dividends is this: ambiguity deserves types, not comments. Nulls and booleans blur meaning. “false,” “zero,” and “we don’t know” are not interchangeable. With modern Java (records, sealed interfaces, pattern matching), I model uncertainty explicitly and make ambiguity impossible to ignore.

Modern Java can express these outcomes as records and sealed types: Present, Missing, and Unverifiable. The same pattern works in ordinary service domains; it does not depend on a scoring model.

The failure mode

You return a number for a score and a boolean “hasEvidence.” A caller subtracts two scores and treats “0” as “no evidence,” then logs an anomaly when “0” appears alongside “hasEvidence=true.” The model caused this. Nulls and booleans encourage shortcuts and misinterpretation.

What I learned

Use records for immutable, transparent domain data

Records let me define concise, immutable carriers without boilerplate. They encourage a bias toward immutability and make the intent clear.

Example response

public record AceuResponse(
ScoreOrUnknown authenticity,
ScoreOrUnknown credibility,
ScoreOrUnknown empathy,
ScoreOrUnknown uniqueness
) {}
public sealed interface ScoreOrUnknown permits Score, Missing, Unverifiable {}
public record Score(double value) implements ScoreOrUnknown {
public Score {
if (Double.isNaN(value) || value < 0.0 || value > 1.0) {
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Score must be [0,1]");
}
}
}
public record Missing(String reason) implements ScoreOrUnknown {}
public record Unverifiable(String note) implements ScoreOrUnknown {}

Records keep the data small and immutable. The sealed hierarchy enforces the set of states at compile time.

Replace nulls and boolean flags with sealed states

The temptation to use Double/Boolean and encode special states with null or false is strong. Resist it. Sealed interfaces make the valid state space explicit and force exhaustive handling. A boolean can’t distinguish “not applicable,” “not yet computed,” and “calculation failed.”

Use pattern matching for exhaustive case handling

Pattern matching in switch makes code read like the domain. It also turns omissions into compile errors when you use exhaustive switches.

Example handler:

public String render(ScoreOrUnknown s) {
return switch (s) {
case Score sc          -> "score=" + sc.value();
case Missing miss      -> "missing=" + miss.reason();
case Unverifiable unv  -> "unverifiable=" + unv.note();

};

}

By handling each case explicitly, I make it impossible to “forget” one or conflate states.

Prefer intent-rich types over ad-hoc maps and strings

When a state needs more context (e.g., why data is missing), capture it in the type. Missing(String reason) and Unverifiable(String note) beat opaque strings and comments. If callers need to act differently based on the reason, add a reason code enum to the record.

Keep aggregates typed—don’t flatten too early

A response with four dimensions should preserve each dimension’s state. Avoid flattening to a single “overall score.” The minute you collapse, you discard information the caller needs for good decisions. In the demo, each dimension returns a ScoreOrUnknown. Only the caller decides how to combine them, and the compiler forces handling of unknowns.

Embed validation where it belongs

Put invariants in the type’s constructor. Scores are [0,1]; reasons should be concise, not multi-paragraph blobs. Records make these guardrails trivial to implement consistently.

Use test fixtures that exercise every branch

Define parameterized tests for your sealed states. For each dimension, test Score, Missing, and Unverifiable. Assert that pattern matching hits each branch, and that any new state added later causes compilation failures in exhaustive switches until it’s handled.

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

More types vs fewer booleans: Sealed types add structure and a few extra classes. The upside is clarity and compile-time enforcement; the downside is minor boilerplate, which records minimize.

Exhaustiveness vs flexibility: Exhaustive switches break on new states until handled. That’s a feature (safety) but can feel strict when you prototype quickly.

Text reasons vs structured codes: Free-form strings are easier; structured enums enable programmatic handling. Choose based on how callers use the data.

Failure modes

“Shadow nulls”

A downstream library returns null and you forget to wrap it in a sealed state. Guard external boundaries with adapters.

“State leakage”: Someone serializes ScoreOrUnknown to a shape that drops the state label (e.g., value=0.0 only). Add JSON configuration that includes a type field and test the wire format.

“Catch-all case”: Using a default branch in pattern matching reintroduces ambiguity. Avoid default; keep exhaustive cases explicit.

Try it yourself

Replace nullable fields for ambiguous states with a sealed interface and record implementations. Add exhaustive pattern matching where you consume them.

Write tests that construct each state per dimension and assert wire-format correctness (e.g., JSON includes the state “type”).

Audit one path where a null sneaks through and add an adapter to convert it into Missing or Unverifiable with a reason code.

  • Records (JEP 395)
  • Sealed Classes (JEP 409)
  • Pattern Matching for switch (JEP 441)

title: Reproducible Java Builds: Pinning, Locking, and Clean-Room Verification
summary: Catch Java build drift before production: dependency pins, lock files, digest references, and clean-room rebuild verification in CI.
author: Shubham Anandani
body:
I’ve seen Java builds succeed locally and differ in CI—transitive dependencies float, plugin versions advance, or caches hide changes. Reproducibility takes intention: pin versions, use lock files, and verify clean-room rebuilds. In a Java build, dependency locks and clean CI environments help reveal resolution drift before artifacts are released.

The failure mode

You set versions in pom.xml but leave transitive ranges unconstrained. Locally, a cached artifact hides a minor release; in CI, it resolves a new version. Behavior changes. The fix is not “rerun until green.” It’s making builds deterministic and verifying them under clean conditions.

What I learned

Pin dependencies and plugins explicitly

Use dependencyManagement to pin versions of critical dependencies and plugins. Avoid wildcard ranges. If you depend on a BOM (bill of materials), understand what it pins and add explicit versions for anything critical that the BOM leaves flexible.

Example

<dependencyManagement>
<dependencies>
<dependency>
<groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
<artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
<version>5.10.2</version>
</dependency>
<!-- pin more -->
</dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

Use a lock mechanism to freeze transitive versions

A lock file captures resolved versions so CI doesn’t “discover” new transitive artifacts. Tools exist for Maven and Gradle that generate and enforce locks. The specifics depend on your chosen plugin; the principle is the same: generate once, commit, and enforce.

Generate lock file locally (or in CI).

Commit it.

Configure the build to fail if resolutions differ from the lock.

Clean-room rebuild in CI

Build in an isolated environment with a cleared local repository. Verify that resolving dependencies succeeds strictly against your lock. Optionally run the build twice—once with the lock (expected success), once with lock enforcement disabled to detect version drift. The second build should fail if drift occurred.

CI steps (illustrative)

- name: Clean local repo
run: rm -rf ~/.m2/repository
- name: Verify dependency locks
run: mvn -q -B clean verify -P enforce-lock
- name: “Clean room” rebuild
run: docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/w" -w /w eclipse-temurin:21-jdk bash -lc "mvn -q -B clean verify -P enforce-lock"

Reproducible artifacts (timestamps and ordering) Ensure JARs are reproducible: strip timestamps, stabilize entry ordering, and avoid embedding environment-specific paths. Many build tools support “reproducible build” flags. Enable them and verify artifact hashes are stable across clean rebuilds.

Digest references for external assets If your build fetches external tools or base images (for integration tests, for example), reference them by digest. Tags are mutable; digests fix identity. The trade-off is manual refresh when security updates appear—worth it for determinism.

Automate updates safely

Use a dependency-update bot that proposes version bumps. Gate those PRs with tests and scanning. Accepting updates becomes explicit, and drift is no longer silent.

Document the “how to fix drift” playbook

When lock enforcement fails, the fix should be documented: regenerate lock with your plugin, review changes, run tests, and commit. Avoid ad-hoc local resolutions—keep the workflow consistent.

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

Pins vs agility: Strict pins and locks slow updates but eliminate surprises. Use bots to keep pace safely.

Clean rooms vs speed: Clean rebuilds take longer. For CI, prioritize correctness over a few minutes of build time.

Digests vs tags: Digests provide determinism; tags ease maintenance. For production-critical assets, default to digests.

Failure modes

“Partial pins”: You pin direct deps but miss transitive ones. Locks solve this; without locks, drift leaks in.

“Plugin drift”: Build plugins advance silently. Pin plugin versions in pluginManagement.

“Non-reproducible JARs”: Differences in timestamps or ordering break hash equality. Turn on reproducible flags and verify.

Try it yourself

Add dependency and plugin pins in dependencyManagement/pluginManagement.

Integrate a lock mechanism; commit the lock file; add an enforcement profile.

Run a clean-room rebuild in CI and compare the artifacts. Confirm artifact hashes match between runs.

  • Gradle dependency locking
  • Reproducible Builds Maven plugin

title: Virtual Threads Changed My Mental Model: Practical Lessons From I/O Fan-Out
summary: Virtual threads simplify I/O fan-out. Learn practical lessons: structured fan-out, back pressure, blocking calls, failure handling, and realistic expectations.
author: Shubham Anandani
body:
Virtual threads changed how I design I/O fan-out in Java services. As an engineering manager who grew up with fixed thread pools, queue sizing, and saturation metrics, I had muscle memory: “pick a pool size, tune it, protect it.” With virtual threads, I can treat blocking I/O more like straightforward code again—without tying throughput to a small pool.

The failure mode

A caller triggers N downstream calls per request (fan-out). With a fixed pool, saturation appears quickly under spikes; with virtual threads, spikes are absorbed but not eliminated. If you translate “we can spawn thousands of threads” into “we don’t need back pressure,” you’ll rediscover failures—just in different places.

What I learned

Think “task-per-thread” for blocking I/O, not “pool-per-service”

Virtual threads make “one virtual thread per blocking task” feasible. You can write linear code for a downstream call and not contort it into callbacks just to avoid blocking. That simplifies failure handling and resource cleanup.

Example fan-out

try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    List<Callable<EvidenceResult>> tasks = sources.stream()
        .map(source -> (Callable<EvidenceResult>) source::fetchEvidence)
        .toList();
    List<Future<EvidenceResult>> futures = executor.invokeAll(tasks);
    List<EvidenceResult> results = new ArrayList<>(futures.size());
    for (Future<EvidenceResult> future : futures) {
        results.add(future.get());
    }
    return aggregate(results);
}

This reads like blocking I/O because it is—but with virtual threads, the scheduler multiplexes them efficiently.

Back pressure still matters

If downstream services or data sources choke under spikes, virtual threads won’t magically fix it. The caller can spin up many virtual threads, but the destination still has limits. You need timeouts, rate limits, and circuit breakers. You also need to avoid accidental fan-in (e.g., mass aggregation that blocks on slowest responders indefinitely).

CPU-bound work belongs elsewhere

Virtual threads help with blocking I/O, not CPU-heavy tasks. If a task saturates CPU, the scheduler can’t help—you need to bound parallelism with a platform-appropriate mechanism (e.g., a limited executor or structured concurrency approach) to avoid oversubscription.

Failure semantics are simpler when code is linear

Exception handling in “straight-line” code is clearer than in callback-based designs. You still need to decide whether partial evidence returns a partial result (with Missing/Unverifiable states) or you fail the whole request. Virtual threads don’t make that decision; they just make the code easier to read.

“Thousands of threads” doesn’t mean “no limits”

Virtual threads are cheap, but not free. Sockets, file descriptors, and memory buffers are finite. The OS still enforces resource ceilings. Guard your fan-out with sensible limits: per-request caps, per-destination timeouts, and global safety checks.

Observability shifts upstream

With fixed pools, saturation appears as queue wait time. With virtual threads, saturation shifts to downstream latency and timeouts. Make sure your metrics capture per-destination latency percentiles and error rates. A spike in virtual-thread creation can be fine if destinations are healthy; it’s not fine if percentiles explode.

Test under synthetic spike and tail latency

I haven’t yet measured performance between virtual threads and a fixed pool for the demo. What I do measure is behavior under artificial spikes: do timeouts fire? Does the aggregation return timely partial results with Missing/Unverifiable? Tests simulate slow destinations and verify we don’t hang.

Timeout per downstream call

try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    Future<EvidenceResult> future = executor.submit(source::fetch);
    try {
        return future.get(timeout.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
    } catch (TimeoutException timeoutError) {
        future.cancel(true);
        return EvidenceResult.unavailable("timeout");
    }
}

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

Simplicity vs explicit limits: Virtual threads reduce boilerplate, but you still must implement back pressure. Silent defaults can mask saturation until it’s too late.

“Everything virtual” vs CPU realities: Virtual threads help with I/O. For CPU-bound work, a bounded executor or workload partitioning is safer.

Observability differences: You lose fixed-pool queue metrics and gain per-destination latency metrics. Update dashboards and alerts accordingly.

Failure modes

“Soft hangs”: Aggregation waits on the slowest responder forever. Add timeouts and partial-return logic.

“Resource leaks”: Thousands of virtual threads keep sockets open longer than intended. Validate resource cleanup paths.

“Oversubscription”: CPU-heavy tasks in virtual threads degrade the whole process. Bound CPU parallelism explicitly.

Try it yourself

Replace a fixed thread pool fan-out with newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() and add per-destination timeouts. Observe behavior under synthetic spikes.

Add aggregation logic that treats timeouts as Missing and downstream errors as Unverifiable. Verify exhaustive handling with pattern matching.

Measure throughput and p95 latency in a controlled environment to inform whether virtual threads help your workload.

  • Virtual Threads (JEP 444)
  • Java 21 ExecutorService API

title: Revocation Is the Hard Part
summary: Revocation checks must avoid “phone home” privacy leaks. Learn lists vs status endpoints, holder stapling, caching, and short-lived credentials.
author: Shubham Anandani
body:
Issuing verifiable credentials is straightforward: define a claim, sign it, return it to the holder. Revocation is harder: you need to detect when a credential should no longer be accepted, ideally without creating a surveillance channel that reveals who asked and when.

The failure mode

A verifier calls a central revocation endpoint for every check. The endpoint sees who asked (IP or key), when, for which credential ID, and what outcome occurred. Even if the credential is privacy-preserving, the revocation lookup becomes a “phone home” channel that leaks context. Users and regulators won’t love that.

What I learned

Understand the revocation design space

Status list (offline)

The issuer publishes a privacy-preserving list of credential status values (for example, a bitstring status list) that verifiers fetch periodically. Verification checks against the local list.

Online status check

The verifier queries a status endpoint per credential. Freshness improves; privacy worsens.

Holder stapling

The holder obtains a fresh status attestation and presents it along with the credential. The verifier checks the stapled proof without contacting the issuer per verification.

Short-lived credentials:

Expire credentials quickly so revocation windows are short. This reduces reliance on revocation checks.

Privacy-preserving lists: batch and compress

A status list can represent many credentials without revealing individual identities. Verifiers download the list on a schedule (e.g., every policy-defined freshness window), cache it locally, and check bits/entries offline. Lists can be partitioned or hashed to limit list size.

Stapling shifts “phone home” to holder flow

With stapling, the holder requests a status proof from the issuer (or a delegated service) at a cadence, then presents it to verifiers. This avoids per-verification lookups by verifiers but still requires the holder to contact the issuer on some schedule. The privacy difference is who calls whom and when.

Short-lived credentials reduce time at risk

If credentials expire quickly, revocation needs are less acute. This shifts load from revocation infrastructure to issuance (more frequent renewals). Combine with holder stapling to keep verification fast and private.

Model cache freshness and failure modes

Verifiers should track the freshness of status lists. If a list is too old (e.g., beyond your policy window), treat the result as “unverifiable” rather than “accepted,” and prompt re-fetch or stapling. Distinguish “cache stale” from “revoked.”

Avoid per-ID URLs in logs

If you must hit an online status endpoint, avoid logging per-ID lookups in a way that identifies a particular holder or verifier. Aggregate metrics instead. Keep any necessary identifiers hashed or pseudonymous.

Distinguish revocation from expiry and audience

Revocation says “this specific credential is no longer valid.” Expiry says “credentials of this type are only valid until T.” Audience says “this verifier is permitted to consume the claim.” Don’t overload revocation with other policy failures.

Illustrative status-list freshness check

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class StatusSnapshot:
    fetched_at: datetime
    bits: bytes

def is_fresh(snapshot: StatusSnapshot, max_age_seconds: int) -> bool:
    age = datetime.now(timezone.utc) - snapshot.fetched_at
    return age.total_seconds() <= max_age_seconds

# Choose the freshness window from policy and operational requirements.
# Stale status should have an explicit outcome, such as "unverifiable".

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

Offline lists vs freshness: Lists preserve privacy but can be stale. Address with frequent, batched updates.

Stapling vs issuer load: Stapling shifts calls to holders; issuer still handles periodic status proofs. Load is manageable with caching and rate limits.

Short-lived credentials vs user friction: Frequent renewals add UX overhead. Balance with clear prompts and automated refresh flows.

Failure modes

“Phone home”: Per-verification lookups leak context. Solution: offline lists or stapling.

“Stale cache”: Verifiers use outdated lists. Solution: freshness checks and policy windows that treat stale as “unverifiable.”

“Revocation conflation”: Treating expiry or audience failure as revocation. Solution: separate policy checks.

Try it yourself

Implement an offline status list with a freshness window. Treat stale lists as “unverifiable.”

Add holder stapling to your demo: the holder fetches a status proof and presents it alongside the credential.

Track performance for offline list checks vs online status calls. Compare privacy and tail behavior.

Further reading

  • Revoke a verifiable credential as an issuer
  • W3C Bitstring Status List v1.0
  • Plan a Verified ID verification solution

title: Null Isn’t False: Building Fair Credential Verifiers
summary: Conflating “missing” with “false” creates bias. Learn a verifier design that separates unverifiable from invalid and protects downstream decisions.
author: Shubham Anandani
body:
One of the subtle but damaging patterns in identity systems is treating null as false. If a credential lacks a field, or a proof is absent, some code paths flip a boolean to false and move on. In verification, this collapses “we don’t know” into “disproven.” The difference matters: missing evidence isn’t proof of falsehood.

The failure mode

A verifier expects a “proofOfX” field. The credential arrives without it. The code sets proofOfX=false. A downstream gate denies access. Later, it turns out “proofOfX” wasn’t required for this flow, or the holder didn’t have a way to request it yet. The deny was based on an absence, not a disproven claim.

What I learned

Model states, not booleans

Replace booleans with intent-rich types. For a given proof, consider states like Present, Missing, Expired, Revoked, Unverifiable (failed binding), and Invalid (malformed or bad signature). This simple taxonomy avoids flattening all “not present” into “false.”

Exhaustive decision logic at boundaries

At the verifier boundary, use exhaustive switches over the state. Force downstream callers to handle each branch. If your language supports pattern matching, lean on it to eliminate default fall-through behaviors.

Treat absence as an opportunity to request or fall back

If a required field is missing, decide whether to:

Prompt the holder to supply it (if applicable).

Proceed with reduced assurance and log the state.

Deny the request explicitly as “unverifiable,” not “invalid.” The right action depends on your policy and context; the key is keeping “unverifiable” distinct.

Make “invalid” a narrow, technical category

Invalid should mean “structured wrong,” “bad signature,” or “contradiction.” It shouldn’t include “not provided,” “not bound,” or “not present yet.” Narrow “invalid” ensures you don’t over-penalize users for the system’s constraints.

Propagate state through APIs and UX

Expose the state in API responses: include status: "unverifiable" with a short note. Avoid returning false or 0 as a sentinel for “missing.” In UX, explain that more evidence is needed or that a different path is available.

Beware implicit type coercions

JSON, databases, and ORMs often coerce nulls to zero or false. Audit these boundaries. Ensure your serializers and persistence layers preserve state labels rather than defaulting values.

Test for fairness: counterfactuals

Put fairness into tests. For example: if “proofOfX” is missing, does the system deny or ask for more evidence? Are there alternative flows? Keep tests that assert the difference between “unverifiable” and “invalid.”

Explicit verification outcomes

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Literal

Status = Literal["accepted", "unverifiable", "invalid"]

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class FieldCheck:
    name: str
    status: Status
    note: str | None = None

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

More state complexity vs simplicity: Explicit states add a little code. The clarity and fairness gains are worth it.

UX friction vs silent denial: Asking for more evidence can add steps. Silent denials are worse. Balance friction with guidance.

Logging granularity vs privacy: Notes improve debugging; ensure they contain no sensitive data.

Failure modes

“Hidden coercion”: Tooling collapses null to false. Solution: audit boundaries and enforce state labels.

“Catch-all invalid”: Development shortcuts treat everything negative as invalid. Solution: write exhaustive switches and linters.

“Unverifiable loop”: Repeated prompts for evidence without alternative paths. Solution: define fallback policies clearly.

Try it yourself

Replace boolean checks for critical credential fields with stateful outcomes (“accepted,” “unverifiable,” “invalid”).

Expose the state in your verifier’s API. Track how often “unverifiable” occurs and address UX with prompts or fallbacks.

Add tests that assert denials only occur for “invalid,” not “unverifiable.”

Further reading

  • W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Model v2.0
  • Java pattern matching for switch
subtitle: Why missing evidence should be “unverifiable,” not “invalid,” and how collapsing those states leads to unfair outcomes.

title: Deploying Identity Services Without a Server to Babysit
summary: Scale-to-zero is great until it isn’t. Learn cold start costs, idle savings, and when identity verifiers need warm instances for predictable latency.
author: Shubham Anandani
body:
Running identity-adjacent services on a scale-to-zero container platform can be delightful: no server to babysit, external HTTPS ingress, and idle billing that doesn’t punish quiet periods. With scale-to-zero containers, quiet periods can reduce idle usage. The trade-off is that the first request after an idle period may be slower, so measure that cold path against the latency needs of the service.

Identity workloads, however, bring constraints: some callers expect predictable latency, and some flows require warm caches or keys ready in memory. The trick is deciding where scale-to-zero helps and where “always on” wins.

The failure mode

You deploy a credential verifier that scales to zero. The first request after an idle period may be much slower than warm requests. A downstream system times out, retries, and amplifies load just as the platform is warming. Worse, your verifier loads keys and trust lists at startup, so the warming step is non-trivial. You saved on idle billing but created unpredictable tails.

What I learned

Cold start budget: measure and design around it

Measure cold starts: container pull, runtime initialization, key load, trust list load, and framework boot. If your end-to-end verification flow includes out-of-process checks (e.g., privacy-preserving revocation lookups), include those too. Decide whether your SLA tolerates the tails; if not, keep a minimum warm replica.

Warm critical paths with lazy loading and caches

Avoid monolithic startup. Load credential-signing keys via a managed secret store, but defer non-critical data until requested. Cache trust lists in memory and refresh asynchronously. Keep proof verification code hot by executing a tiny “self-check” during startup.

Set min replicas for latency-sensitive endpoints

If your platform supports minimum replicas, keep one verifier instance warm. Scale additional instances on demand. This hybrid approach preserves predictable latency while retaining cost controls.

Health, readiness, and the “thin ready” trap

Identity verifiers shouldn’t mark “ready” until critical dependencies (keys, trust lists) are present and a test proof passes. A “thin ready” (bare process up) can route traffic to a half-initialized instance, increasing failure rates.

Scale rules: event triggers vs queue length

If you use event-driven scale, ensure triggers reflect verifier load. Queue length or request rate are better signals than raw CPU in a verifier, since cryptographic checks are sporadic and short. Use conservative ramp-up to avoid stampedes during traffic bursts.

Idle billing: cost vs safety

Scale-to-zero saves money during periods of inactivity. In identity systems, weigh this against the cost of false timeouts and retries. For certain flows (e.g., login or checkout proofs), unpredictable tails are more expensive than idle replicas.

Pipeline hygiene: small image, quick pull

Use multi-stage builds, slim bases, and .dockerignore to keep images small. The smaller the image, the faster cold start. Avoid compiling dependencies at startup; freeze them in the image. Keep secrets out of layers entirely (next article).

Illustrative configuration

# Generic container-app.yaml structure
name: identity-service
ingress:
  external: true
  targetPort: 8000
template:
  containers:
    - image: your-registry/identity-service:tag
      resources:
        cpu: 0.5
        memory: 0.5Gi
  probes:
    liveness:
      httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8000 }
    readiness:
      httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8000 }
  scale:
    minReplicas: 1 # Keep one warm replica
    maxReplicas: 10
    rules:
      - name: http-requests
        http: { metadata: { concurrentRequests: "50" } }

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

Cost vs predictability: Scale-to-zero cuts idle spend but risks unpredictable tails. Hybrid min replicas often balance both.

Strict readiness vs fast green: Stricter readiness delays routing but avoids half-initialized failures. Bias toward strict in identity contexts.

Lazy load vs startup completeness: Deferring non-critical data speeds boot but adds first-request work. Choose wisely.

Failure modes

“Thin ready”: Traffic routed to instances without loaded keys or trust lists. Fix readiness to validate critical paths.

“Stampede”: Traffic surge triggers too many replicas and cache thrash. Fix scale rules and backpressure.

“Oversized image”: Cold starts dominated by image pulls. Fix Docker hygiene.

Try it yourself

Measure the cold start path and identify high-cost steps. Record cold-start and warm-request latency as separate measurements.

Add a minimum warm replica and track tails. Compare p95 across scale-to-zero vs hybrid.

Implement readiness that runs a tiny proof self-check and confirms secret load before returning ready.

Further reading

  • Scale applications in Azure Container Apps
  • Health probes in Azure Container Apps

title: Verifiable Doesn’t Mean Verified: Getting Issuer, Holder, and Verifier Right
summary: Verifiable credentials can be signed and valid yet still wrong. Learn issuer/holder/verifier roles, failure modes, and checks beyond JSON and signatures.
author: Shubham Anandani
body:
I’m an engineering manager with experience integrating identity-verification flows conceptually aligned with Microsoft Entra Verified ID. One habit that keeps teams honest is repeating the phrase: verifiable doesn’t mean verified. The W3C Verifiable Credentials data model makes claims portable and cryptographically provable, but it doesn’t magically make those claims true, up to date, or appropriate for your use case.

The failure mode

A team builds a credential verifier that checks JSON shape and a signature. The code reports “valid.” A downstream feature treats the claim as true. Weeks later, someone discovers the issuer did, in fact, sign the credential, but the subject was not the person currently presenting it, or the credential expired months ago. The failure wasn’t cryptography; it was process: treating “verifiable” as “verified.”

What I learned

Roles and responsibilities: issuer, holder, verifier

Issuer: Asserts something about a subject (the holder) and signs the assertion. Their trustworthiness is a human, contractual, and policy question, not a purely technical one.
Holder: Receives and stores the credential; presents it to a verifier. Binding the holder to the subject of the credential (is this person who the claim describes?) is a separate step.
Verifier: Evaluates signature validity, checks schema, ensures the issuer is trusted for that claim type, confirms the subject binding, interprets policy (expiry, audience, revocation), and decides whether to accept the claim.

Well-formed is necessary but not sufficient

A credential can be:

Well-formed: It conforms to expected JSON structure.
Signed: The cryptographic proof validates against the issuer’s public key.
Trusted: The issuer is recognized and allowed to assert this particular claim type.
Bound: The subject is provably the presenter.
Current: It hasn’t expired and isn’t revoked. Only when all are satisfied does “valid” approach “usable.”

Separate signature validation from trust decision

Cryptography answers “did the claimed issuer sign this payload?” Trust answers “do we trust this issuer for this claim type right now?” You need both. If the issuer isn’t in your trust registry for the claim being evaluated, the result shouldn’t be “invalid claim,” it should be “untrusted issuer for this policy.”

Subject binding is a first-class step

A classic failure mode: someone presents a signed credential about a subject, but the presenter isn’t the subject. In practical flows, the verifier should confirm that the presenter’s wallet or identity key pair matches the credential subject, or use an out-of-band binding method aligned with your policy. If binding is missing, treat the result as “unverifiable” rather than “false.”

Expiry and audience are policy gates, not parsing details

Expiry and audience are part of the claim semantics. A credential can be signed and well-formed yet expired (or intended for a different audience). These conditions should result in “policy failure” states distinct from “cryptographic failure.”

Revocation closes the loop

Issuance is easy; ensuring the claim is still valid is the hard part. Revocation checks must avoid “phone home” privacy leaks (more in the revocation article below). Even a toy system benefits from an offline revocation list or privacy-preserving status check.

Distinguish “invalid” from “unverifiable”

Illustrative verification flow

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Literal

Status = Literal["accepted", "unverifiable", "invalid"]

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ValidationResult:
    signature_valid: bool
    issuer_trusted: bool
    subject_bound: bool
    policy_ok: bool
    status: Status

# Keep proof validation, issuer trust, subject binding, and policy checks separate.
# The exact proof checks depend on the credential format and verifier library supported by the deployment.

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

Strict policy gates vs user friction: Strong audience/expiry checks reduce misuse but can frustrate users who present slightly out-of-date credentials. The fix is short-lived credentials and good UX.

Offline trust lists vs dynamic fetch: Offline lists avoid privacy leaks but risk staleness. Consider periodic sync with no per-verification lookups.

Subject binding rigor vs simplicity: Strong binding reduces fraud but adds ceremony. Pick the approach that fits your risk.

Failure modes

“Signed, therefore true”: Conflating cryptographic validity with trust. Fix by separating proof validation from issuer trust policy.

“Presenter ≠ subject”: Accepting credentials without subject binding. Fix by explicit binding checks.

“Policy drift”: Undocumented audience/expiry rules. Fix with centralized policy and tests.

Try it yourself

Implement a verifier that separately evaluates cryptographic proof, issuer trust, subject binding, and policy gates.

Return “unverifiable” for missing binding and “invalid” for failed policy (e.g., expiry).

Measure performance across well-formed accepts vs policy failures to understand user impact.

Further reading

  • W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Model v2.0
  • Microsoft Entra Verified ID verification planning
  • Configure a Verified ID verifier

title: Keys Don’t Belong in the Image: Secret Management for Credential Signing
summary: Keep signing keys out of images. Learn managed secret stores, rotation, mounts, and CI/scan steps that catch accidental key bake-ins before deploy.
author: Shubham Anandani
body:
Signing keys are crown jewels in identity services. If they leak, attackers can mint forged credentials that look real. The easiest way to leak a key is to bake it into a container image or configuration file. Load signing keys at runtime from a managed secret store; keep private key material out of source files, build arguments, and image layers.

The failure mode

A contributor tests locally with a .env file containing a signing key. A sloppy Dockerfile copies everything under the project directory, including .env. CI builds the image; the key ends up in a layer. The image is pushed to a registry. Even if you rotate later, the leak is permanent in history.

What I learned

Secrets never live in source or image layers

Keep signing keys out of your repository and artifact layers. Use a managed secret store pattern to provide keys at runtime via secure mounts or platform-managed environment variables that never touch the image.

.dockerignore is a security control

Treat .dockerignore as part of your security posture. Explicitly ignore .env, credential files, test fixtures containing secrets, and local caches. Keep the build context as small as possible.

Runtime retrieval, not build-time embedding

Load keys at runtime from the secret store client library or a platform-provided mount. Fail readiness until the key loads. If the secret is missing, return clear errors and refuse to sign. Do not “fall back” to dummy keys in production—reserve test keys for explicit non-prod builds.

Rotation: short lifetimes and multiple active keys

Signing keys should rotate regularly. The verifier should accept signatures from a small set of current keys, and the issuer should roll keys with overlap: publish new key, start signing with it, keep the old key valid for verification until the overlap window expires.

Audit and scanning: prevent accidental bake-ins

Add CI checks that scan images for secret patterns. Simple rules catch common mistakes (e.g., files named .env, PEM key headers). Block the build if found. Complement this with code scanning that flags dangerous COPY patterns.

Separate test and prod key handling

For demos, use explicitly marked test keys with sandboxed scopes. Never reuse test keys in environments accessible outside controlled demos. Label logs and status endpoints so it’s obvious which environment your verifier belongs to.

Minimize key surface: hardware-backed or managed services

Where possible, use hardware-backed key stores or provider-managed keys with restricted export. Keep application access tightly scoped to “sign” and “read public key.” The app should never be able to exfiltrate private key material.

Illustrative runtime secret loading

def load_signing_key(secret_store, key_id: str) -> bytes:
    key = secret_store.read(key_id)
    if not key:
        raise RuntimeError("signing key unavailable")
    return key

# Load keys from a managed store at runtime. Never copy key material
# into source, build arguments, container layers, or sample configuration.
# Keep readiness false until the signing dependency is ready.

Example .dockerignore

.env
*.pem
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.git/
node_modules/
tests/fixtures/secrets/

Example Dockerfile pattern

FROM python:3.12-slim AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
COPY pyproject.toml poetry.lock ./
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir poetry && poetry install --no-root
COPY --chown=10001:10001 app ./app
USER 10001
EXPOSE 8000

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

Runtime dependency vs build independence: Secret store clients add runtime requirements. The gain is eliminating baked-in risk.

Rotation complexity vs safety: Overlapping keys complicate issuers and verifiers. The gain is smooth migration.

Strict readiness vs availability: Refusing to start without keys prevents undefined behavior. Availability dips are better than silent mis-signing.

Failure modes

“COPY .”: Blindly copying the entire source tree into the image. Fix with .dockerignore and explicit COPY.

“Fallback key”: Using a dummy key in production when secret load fails. Fix with hard failures and improved observability.

“Exportable private keys”: Allowing the app to export private keys. Fix with hardware-backed or provider-managed keys.
